Part E · Chapter 1

Vision transformers and image tokens

Cut a photo into patches, turn the patches into tokens, and read them with a transformer

A vision transformer (ViT) reads a photo as a language model reads text, once the photo is cut into patches that become vectors. This chapter covers position embeddings, the class token, where a patch looks, ViT against convolutional networks (CNNs), and image tokens. The figures use a ViT-B/16 on shark photos, and it often names sharks wrongly because ImageNet has only three shark classes. Photos are credited under the figures.

You will need: the transformer block and attention (D5, D4), the embedding table (D2), filters and receptive fields (C1, C2), and matrix products (0.5).

Cutting a photo into patches

Guess first. A photo of 224 by 224 pixels has 50,176 pixels, so one token per pixel would make attention compare all pairs of tokens, as in the attention chapter. How many pairs is that, and what could you use as a token instead?

A vision transformer (ViT) is a transformer whose tokens are patches: square blocks of pixels cut from the photo. Here P is the patch side in pixels, and in ViT-B/16, the base-size ViT, P = 16. A 224 by 224 photo then gives 14 patches across and 14 down, so attention compares about 200 tokens instead of 50,176 pixels. Attention scores all pairs of tokens, once per attention head (one of the parallel attention computations of a block). So its cost grows with the square of the sequence length, the number of tokens.

  1. Drag Patch side P to 8 px. The boxes under the picture change to 784 patches and 616,225 attention pairs per head, from 196 patches and 38,809 pairs at 16 px.
  2. Set it back to 16 px and press Step: one patch lifts from the grid into the row of tokens, and its position number appears below it.

Halving the patch side from 16 to 8 pixels gives four times as many patches (196 to 784) and 15.9 times as many attention pairs per head.

How it works

Take P = 16. The photo has side S = 224 pixels, so 224 / 16 = 14 patches fit across and 14 down, and N = 14 × 14 = 196. A pixel has three numbers (red, green and blue), so a patch of 16 × 16 pixels has 16 × 16 × 3 = 768 numbers. The ViT also adds one extra token, the class token (a learned vector without pixels), so the sequence length is n = N + 1 = 197. One attention head then scores 1972 = 38,809 pairs, while one pixel per token would give 50,1762 = 2,517,630,976 pairs, about 65,000 times more. The Go deeper section below has the NumPy code for the cut.

224 / 16patches across, S / P×224 / 16patches down=196patches, N|768numbers in a patch, P × P × 3|197²pairs per head, n² with n = N + 1

Common belief. Smaller patches always give a better view of the shark, so use the smallest.

Why it fails. The cost of attention grows with the square of N, so from P = 16 to P = 8 the pairs grow 15.9 times. Halving P also cuts the numbers in a patch from 768 to 192, so a token describes a smaller part of the photo.

Better account. The patch side trades detail against cost. The ViT paper (Dosovitskiy and others, 2021) notes that smaller patches cost more computation, and people choose P to fit the compute they have.

Quick quiz

How many patches does a 224 by 224 photo give with P = 32, and how many numbers does a patch have?

Since 224 / 32 = 7, there are 7 × 7 = 49 patches. A patch has 32 × 32 × 3 = 3,072 numbers. The total is 49 × 3,072 = 150,528, which is 224 × 224 × 3, so the cut loses no number.

Why does attention over patches cost about 16 times more when P goes from 16 to 8?

N grows four times, since both the number across and the number down double. Attention compares all pairs, so its cost grows with the square of the sequence: 4 × 4 = 16, or 15.9 once the class token is counted.

Reading the figure

Move the slider, then press Step or Play. A patch is lifted from the grid into the row, and its position number appears below it. The numbers run in reading order, from the left of the top row to the right of the bottom row. The row shows the first nine tokens and the last, because 196 tokens do not fit on a screen. Tick the box and the class token takes position 0 (the class token section explains it).

A second case, P = 8

A second case, P = 8. Now N = 28 × 28 = 784 patches of 192 numbers. The sequence has 785 tokens and 616,225 pairs per head, which is 15.9 times as many as for P = 16. The photo has 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 numbers for any patch size, and 784 × 192 is again 150,528, so the cut loses no numbers. What changes is how much the later blocks must handle.

Symbols

\[ N = \frac{S}{P}\cdot\frac{S}{P} = \frac{S^2}{P^2},\qquad \text{numbers per patch} = P^2 C,\qquad n = N + 1,\qquad \text{pairs per head} = n^2 \]

  • \(S\) is the side of the photo in pixels (224 here, a square photo) and \(P\) the side of a patch. \(C\) is the number of colour channels, 3 (C1).
  • \(N\) is the number of patches. \(n\) is the sequence length with the class token added; \(n\) matches the symbol of D4, where attention costs grow like \(n^2\).

Where the cut is crude

A patch of 16 pixels is cut without regard to what is in it, so a fin can be split over four patches, and the later blocks must put the pieces together again. Attention is how the model can combine them. A small animal is a problem. A shark 60 pixels long in a photo 640 pixels wide is about 20 pixels long after the photo is resized to 224, which is little more than one patch. The patch side is part of the name of a model, and it affects the cost. ViT-B/32 has 49 patches and ViT-B/16 has 196, and in torchvision's counts the second needs about four times the work (the count is in ViT against CNN).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When you cut a photo with NumPy, check the order of the axes. img.reshape(196, 768) on its own gives strips of 768 consecutive numbers (one image row and the start of the next), not patches. The cut needs a reshape into (14, 16, 14, 16, 3), a transpose of the middle axes, and then a reshape. Test it: patch 1 must equal img[0:16, 16:32].

In Python

import numpy as np
S, P, C = 224, 16, 3
img = np.arange(S * S * C).reshape(S, S, C) % 251     # a made-up picture, values 0 to 250
g = S // P
patches = img.reshape(g, P, g, P, C).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4).reshape(g * g, P * P * C)
print(patches.shape)
print(np.array_equal(patches[1], img[0:16, 16:32].reshape(-1)))
print(patches.size == img.size)
for P in (8, 16, 32):
    N = (S // P) ** 2
    print(P, N, N + 1, (N + 1) ** 2)
(196, 768)
True

From a patch to a token

Guess first. A patch of 16 by 16 pixels with three colours has 768 numbers, and the vectors inside ViT-B/16 also have 768 numbers. Is the patch already the token, or does something still happen to it, and what is the simplest operation that could do it?

A patch becomes a token by a linear projection, a matrix product plus a bias. The matrix Wpatch has 768 rows, and a row is a filter of 16 × 16 × 3 weights laid over the patch. Number j of the token is the dot product of row j with the patch's 768 pixel numbers x (multiply matching numbers, then add) plus a bias bj. The vector of these d = 768 numbers is the patch embedding, where d is the model width. Since one matrix is used for all 196 non-overlapping patches, this is a convolution with 768 filters of 16 by 16 and a step of 16.

  1. Find the patch in the coral frame on the shark's body (row 6, column 6, counting from 0). The colour pictures are rows of Wpatch, and the number beside a picture is its result: 0.04 for row 143 and −0.30 for row 402.
  2. Click the water patch in the top left corner: row 63 changes from −0.11 to 0.16, and the others change too.

Click a patch (or use the arrow keys)

The patch, 16 by 16 pixels, and its 768 numbers laid out in 16 rows of 48 (three cells, red, green and blue, for a pixel)

Eight of the 768 rows of the matrix, drawn as colour pictures, multiplied with the patch numbers and added to a bias

Sizes for a patch side P (the live numbers above are for P = 16)

The 768 numbers of a token are 768 dot products of the patch with the 768 rows, and the same rows are used on all 196 patches.

How it works

Take the patch at grid row 6, column 6 of the hammerhead photo (cropped to a square and resized to 224 by 224 pixels). The patch's 768 pixel numbers, scaled as the network expects, form the list x. For red, green and blue, the scaling subtracts a fixed mean and divides by a fixed standard deviation, both taken from the training photos. Row 143 of Wpatch has 768 weights. Its dot product with x, plus the bias 0.0077, gives 0.04, one of the 768 numbers of the token e.

768×1token e=768×768Wpatch, 589,824 weights×768×1x, the flat patch+768×1bias b

The matrix has 768 × 768 = 589,824 weights, and with the 768 biases that makes 590,592 numbers learned in training, whatever the number of patches. Because one matrix is shared, an edge or a colour is read in the same way wherever it lies, and only one matrix is learned.

Analogy. In the embedding table of the embeddings chapter, a token ID picks a row, and the row is its vector. Here the patch plays the part of the ID and the token e the part of the row.

Where it breaks. A table has one row per known token. There is no table of patches, since there are 256768 possible patches. The matrix gives a vector to any patch, including one never seen, and patches with similar pixels get similar vectors. The matrix is a function that computes a vector, where a table is a dictionary that looks one up.

Quick quiz

With P = 32, how many columns does the patch matrix have, and how many weights?

A patch has 32 × 32 × 3 = 3,072 numbers, so the matrix has 3,072 columns and 768 rows: 2,359,296 weights, plus 768 biases. A larger patch gives a larger matrix and fewer tokens.

Why is the same matrix used for all patches?

So that a feature found in one part of the photo can be found in another, as with a filter that slides over a photo in a convolution. It also keeps the count of weights small: one matrix and not 196.

Go deeper second patch, symbols, cost, Python about 3 min

Reading the figure

The weights in the figure are the first layer of torchvision's ViT-B/16. The page takes the pixels of the selected patch, scales them as the network expects (subtract the mean, divide by the spread of the colour), and computes eight of the 768 dot products itself. The results agree with the network's own output to within 0.003. In the grid of the patch's 768 numbers and in the bars, teal is positive and coral is negative. Some rows look smooth and some look like noise. Try the patch in the water and then a patch on the body: the eight values change, because they are computed from the pixels of the selected patch. They are eight of the 768 numbers of the patch embedding.

Two patches, eight numbers

Two worked cases for the hammerhead photo. The patch at grid row 6, column 6 lies on the body. Its eight numbers are 0.04, −0.05, −0.11, 0.09, −0.10, −0.30, 0.09 and 0.22. The patch in the top left corner is blue water. Its eight numbers are −0.08, 0.05, 0.16, −0.09, −0.03, 0.05, −0.04 and −0.02. The two sets differ, and the matrix has 760 more rows that the figure does not show.

Symbols

\[ \mathbf{e}_i = W_{\text{patch}}\,\mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{b},\qquad W_{\text{patch}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times P^2C},\qquad \mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{P^2C} \]

  • \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is patch \(i\) flattened into a list of \(P^2C = 768\) numbers, row by row, three colours per pixel. \(\mathbf{e}_i\) is its embedding, with \(d = 768\) numbers.
  • \(W_{\text{patch}}\) has \(d\) rows and \(P^2C\) columns. Row \(j\) is a filter of 16 by 16 by 3 weights, and output number \(j\) is its dot product with the patch plus \(b_j\). The matrix and the bias are learned with the rest of the network (B4).
  • The count of learned numbers is \(d\,P^2C + d = 589{,}824 + 768 = 590{,}592\). In C1 terms, a convolution with 768 filters of 16 by 16 on 3 channels has \((16\cdot16\cdot3+1)\cdot768 = 590{,}592\) weights. With a step of 16 it gives \((224-16)/16+1 = 14\) positions across.

Why a linear map, and where it is limited

The first block needs vectors, and a linear map is the plainest way to get them. It is cheap: one patch costs 589,824 multiply-adds (a weight times a pixel number, added to a running sum), and the whole photo 115,605,504, the same for P = 8, 16 or 32, because a pixel number meets 768 weights once. The cost that depends on P comes later, in the blocks. The matrix sees one patch at a time, so it cannot know about the neighbouring patch. All use of context is left to attention.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a pretrained ViT returns confident nonsense on your own photo, print the mean and spread of the input after scaling. They should be near 0 and 1 for red, green and blue. A network trained on scaled pixels given values from 0 to 255 produces tokens about a hundred times too large. Check also that the colour order is red, green, blue and not blue, green, red.

In Python

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
img = rng.integers(0, 256, size=(224, 224, 3)).astype(float)
patches = img.reshape(14, 16, 14, 16, 3).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4).reshape(196, 768)
W = rng.normal(0, 0.02, size=(768, 768))     # made-up weights: one row per output number
b = np.zeros(768)
tokens = patches @ W.T + b
print(tokens.shape, W.size + b.size)
w0 = W[0].reshape(16, 16, 3)                 # row 0 as a 16 by 16 by 3 filter
by_hand = (img[0:16, 16:32] * w0).sum() + b[0]
print(np.isclose(tokens[1, 0], by_hand))
print(768 * 768 * 196)
(196, 768) 590592
True

Position embeddings

Guess first. A ViT adds a learned vector, a position embedding, to the token of the patch. After training, how alike do you expect the vectors of two neighbouring positions to be, and how alike those of positions in opposite corners?

Attention alone cannot tell where a patch came from: reordering the tokens only reorders the outputs, so attention treats the patches as a set, a collection without order. The position embeddings come from a learned table of 197 rows of 768 numbers, one row for the class token and 196 for the patch positions. To see what the table has learned, we compare two of its rows by their cosine similarity. It is 1 when the vectors point the same way, 0 at a right angle and −1 when they are opposite.

  1. Read the map: teal squares have a position vector similar to the chosen one (outlined in coral in the photo and in black in the map), and coral squares one that points away from it. At row 6, column 6 the cosine similarity is 0.59 to the next patch along the row and −0.66 to the farthest corner.
  2. Click other squares: the teal squares tend to line up along the row and the column of the chosen square.

A. The position table of the trained ViT: click a position and see how similar the other 195 positions are to it

Photo (for orientation)

Cosine similarity of position embeddings

Positions one patch apart have a mean cosine similarity of 0.73, and positions three apart are more alike in the same column (0.43) or row (0.22) than when they share neither (−0.04).

How it works

Take the patch at row 6, column 6, which is position 91 because the class token is position 0. Its input to the first block is the sum of its patch embedding and row 91 of the table, added number by number. Attention computes its scores from this sum, so the same patch at another position can get other scores. To test how much the ViT relies on position, we move patches to other places and keep the position vectors where they are. A run is one photo in one random order. We count the runs whose top call (the class with the highest probability) is the same as for the unmoved photo, right or wrong.

768×1input z of token 91=768×1patch embedding e+768×1row 91 of the table Epos|197×768Epos: 151,296 numbers
  1. Predict first what happens to the ViT's top call when patches are moved to other places and the position vectors stay put. Predict also what ResNet-18, a CNN (convolutional network) of 18 layers, would do.
  2. Drag Patches moved, k, to 32. The text under the plot says that the top call is unchanged in 69% of the runs for the ViT and 31% for ResNet-18 (14 photos × 16 random orders).
  3. Drag k to 196. The ViT keeps its call in 29% of the runs and ResNet-18 in 0%, and the hammerhead photo is still called “hammerhead”, with probability 39%.

B. Move patches: the first k patches of a fixed random order are passed along in a circle, and the position vectors stay where they are

Common belief. A ViT can name a shark only if it knows the layout: fins above, tail behind.

Why it fails. With all patches moved, the hammerhead photo still gets the call “hammerhead”, now with probability 39% (88% when unmoved). Over the 14 photos, the ViT keeps its call in 29% of the runs and ResNet-18 in none, so it changes its call in most runs.

Better account. Position embeddings encode layout, which matters for tasks that ask where (finding the shark, counting animals), and this test did not try them. For a single label, patch contents can give part of the answer. This fits the 29%: a moved patch keeps its colour, its texture and the part of an outline inside it.

Quick quiz

Why does attention without positions treat the patches as a set?

An output is a weighted sum over all tokens, with weights computed from the query and key vectors of the tokens. Reorder the tokens and the sums keep the same terms, so the outputs are the same vectors in a new order.

A ViT keeps its top call in 29% of the runs when all patches are moved. Does that prove positions are useless?

No. It shows that for a one-word label of these 14 photos the patch contents give part of the answer. Tasks that depend on layout were not tested.

Go deeper symbols, table structure, test details, Python about 4 min

Why attention alone treats the patches as a set

Without a position vector, the model would treat the 196 patches as a set, a bag of patches: it would use what the patches contain and not where they are. This can be shown in two lines. Attention (D4) computes an output as a weighted sum of values, with weights from query-key dot products. If you reorder the input tokens (a permutation of the list), the same sums are formed from the same numbers. The outputs then come out reordered in the same way and are otherwise unchanged. The code at the end of this fold checks it. Adding a position vector breaks this symmetry: patch content moves, position vectors stay, and the outputs generally differ (the code shows one case).

Symbols

\[ \mathbf{z}^{(0)}_i = \mathbf{e}_i + E_{\text{pos}}[i],\qquad E_{\text{pos}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d} \]

  • \(\mathbf{z}^{(0)}_i\) is the input of token \(i\) to the first block. \(\mathbf{e}_i\) is its patch embedding from the last section.
  • \(E_{\text{pos}}\) is a table like the embedding table of D2: one row per place, with \(N + 1\) rows because the class token has a place too. For ViT-B/16 it has \(197\times768 = 151{,}296\) numbers, learned with the rest of the network (the 2017 transformer used the fixed sinusoids of D5 instead).

What the table looks like

The table has structure, and no rule about distance was written into the model: training produced it. Over all pairs of patch positions, two positions one patch apart have an average cosine of 0.73. For positions 3 apart it is 0.33, and for positions 10 apart −0.05. These are pairs whose centres are 1, 3 or 10 patches apart: all pairs at distance 1 and at distance 3 share a row or a column, and 112 of the 304 pairs at distance 10 do. Same-row pairs 3 columns apart average 0.22, same-column pairs 3 rows apart about 0.43 (computed from the stored map), and pairs about as far apart that share neither row nor column −0.04. The ViT paper reports the same two features, closeness and a row and column pattern (Dosovitskiy and others, 2021). The fall with distance is not smooth: pairs 6 apart average 0.38, which is more than the 0.33 of pairs 3 apart. The paper notes a sinusoidal look in the position tables of larger grids, and this may be the same effect.

Reading the patch-moving result

The plotted result is an average over 14 photos and 16 random orders (224 runs per point) for one ViT, so it does not show that positions are useless. The 14 pictures are the shark photo set: eight shark photos, two drawings of the Ganges shark and four photos of other animals. The unmoved call is wrong for some of them: the ViT calls both milk shark photos “hammerhead”. At 16 patches moved the ViT keeps its call 76% of the time and ResNet-18 51%. At 64 moved: 66% and 16%. At 128 moved: 38% and 0%. In this test the ViT depends less on where a patch is than ResNet-18 does, which suggests that it relies more on what the patches contain, such as colour and texture. A study of DeiT models reached a similar conclusion (Naseer and others, 2021). The two networks were also trained with different recipes (torchvision's ViT-B/16 uses a modified DeiT recipe, ResNet-18 a simple one), so this run cannot separate architecture from training.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If you feed a ViT a photo of a different size, the number of patches changes and the position table no longer has the right number of rows. Libraries resize the table by interpolating the patch rows in two dimensions. The class token's row must stay at index 0 and not be interpolated.

In Python

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
n, d = 5, 4
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(d, d)) for _ in range(3))
def attend(X):
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    s = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    w = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True)); w /= w.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ V
perm = np.array([3, 0, 4, 1, 2])
print(np.allclose(attend(X)[perm], attend(X[perm])))              # reorder the tokens: the outputs reorder
pos = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
print(np.allclose(attend(X + pos)[perm], attend(X[perm] + pos)))  # tokens move, positions stay: the outputs differ
True
False

The class token

Guess first. A transformer gives back one vector per token, so 196 vectors for 196 patches. A classifier needs one vector for the photo. Would you average the patch vectors, use the middle patch, or something else?

The class token is one extra token placed before the patches. It starts as a learned vector of 768 numbers with no pixels in it. The blocks treat it like the other tokens, so attention lets it gather information from the patches. After the last block, a linear layer called the head turns its vector into 1,000 scores. There is one score per class of ImageNet, the labelled photo set used to train this network. The head is not an attention head and reads only this vector.

  1. Drag Block from 11 down to 0. The shading shows where the class token reads (an average over the 12 heads of the block). The coral box counts how many patches, brightest first, it takes to reach half of the class token's attention to patches. It is 10 at block 11, 42 at block 2 and 97 at block 0.
  2. Choose the grey bamboo shark photo: the diagram ends with “electric ray 56%”, and ImageNet has no bamboo shark class.

For the hammerhead photo, half of the class token's attention to patches needs 97 patches at block 0 but only 10 at block 11.

How it works

Take the hammerhead photo. Its 197 tokens, the class token and 196 patches, pass through 12 blocks. After block 11 and a final layer norm (it centres and rescales the 768 numbers), the class token's vector y has 768 numbers. The head multiplies y by a matrix with 1,000 rows and 768 columns and adds 1,000 biases, which is 768 × 1,000 + 1,000 = 769,000 numbers learned. A softmax turns the 1,000 scores into probabilities that add up to 1 (a larger score gets a larger probability), and the largest, 88%, is for “hammerhead”.

1,000×1scores=1,000×768Whead×768×1y, class vector after the last norm+1,000×1bias

A bright patch shows where the class token read, which need not be where the evidence for the answer lies. Flattening the attention of the last block means giving all 197 tokens the same weight. It changes the hammerhead probability only from 88% to 81% (the explaining chapter runs this test on the same network, with the photo squashed to 224 by 224 pixels).

Common belief. The class token is a special part of the model that looks at the picture.

Why it fails. The blocks give it no weights of its own, so to them it is one more token. It has a starting vector and a row of the position table, and the same attention and feed-forward weights act on it as on any other token. The feed-forward part, or MLP, is a small network applied to the tokens one at a time.

Better account. It is a place to put an answer. Attention gives it a way to gather from the patches, and the weights set by training determine what it gathers.

Quick quiz

How many tokens does ViT-B/16 read for a 224 by 224 photo, and which one is read by the classifier?

The sequence has 197 tokens: the 196 patches and the class token. The classifier reads only the class token after the last block.

The class token has no pixels. How can its final vector depend on the photo?

In the blocks, attention lets it read the patch tokens, and the MLP and later blocks work on what it read. Its start is the same for all photos, and the difference comes from the patches.

Go deeper symbols, other readouts, Python about 3 min

Reading the figure

The maps are averages over the 12 heads of a block, and the brightest patch is drawn fully bright in all blocks.

Slide the block from 0 to 11. The class token goes through the same blocks, with the same weights, as the patch tokens. In a block it reads the patches (this is the map) and the patches may read it. In the hammerhead photo, 97 patches are needed to reach half of its patch attention at block 0, 42 at block 2 and 10 at block 11. In the same blocks it also puts 21% (block 0), 57% (block 2) and 37% (block 11) of its weight on itself, which is the first number in the boxes.

From the class vector to the call

The class token starts with the same learned vector for all photos, so any difference in its final vector comes from what it read. After the 12th block, torchvision applies a layer norm and a linear layer with 768 × 1,000 + 1,000 = 769,000 numbers. For the hammerhead photo the largest of the 1,000 probabilities is “hammerhead” at 88%. The same network calls the grey bamboo shark in its tank an electric ray (56%), and the spadenose photo an eel (31%). ImageNet has three shark classes (great white, tiger, hammerhead), so spadenose and bamboo sharks have no label of their own.

Symbols

\[ \mathbf{z}^{(0)}_0 = \mathbf{x}_{\text{class}} + E_{\text{pos}}[0],\qquad \mathbf{y} = \mathrm{LN}\big(\mathbf{z}^{(L)}_0\big),\qquad \text{scores} = W_{\text{head}}\,\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{b}_{\text{head}} \]

  • \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{class}}\) is the learned starting vector of the class token, with 768 numbers (the ViT paper writes it the same way), and \(E_{\text{pos}}[0]\) is the first row of the position table, added as for the patches. \(L\) is the number of blocks, 12, so \(\mathbf{z}^{(L)}_0\) is the class token after the last block.
  • \(\mathrm{LN}\) is layer norm (B6). The scores go through softmax as in A3 to give the probabilities.

Other readouts

Taking the answer out of the network, here from the class token, is the readout. The class token is one design choice among others. The ViT paper compares it with averaging the patch vectors, and finds that both work similarly once the learning rate is tuned for the two designs.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Averaging the patch vectors gives a usable summary, but a head trained on the class token will not work on the average without training. If the readout differs between training and use, accuracy drops and no error message appears.

In Python

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
d, n_classes = 768, 1000
y = rng.normal(size=d)                                  # the class vector after the last norm (made-up numbers)
W = rng.normal(0, 0.02, size=(n_classes, d))            # made-up head, one row per class
b = np.zeros(n_classes)
scores = W @ y + b
p = np.exp(scores - scores.max()); p /= p.sum()
print(scores.shape, W.size + b.size)
print(round(float(p.sum()), 3), int(p.argmax()), round(float(p.max()), 3))
(1000,) 769000
1.0 749 0.006

The head turns 768 numbers into 1,000 scores. The numbers here are made up, so the winning class tells you little. With a trained head the winner is the call of the network.

Where a patch looks

Guess first. A 3 by 3 convolution layer reads a 3 by 3 window. In the first block of a ViT, a patch can attend to all 196 patches (itself included) and the class token. Do you expect the heads there to look mostly at neighbours, or all over the photo?

An attention head is one of the parallel attention computations of a block, and ViT-B/16 has 12 per block. L2H5 means block 2, head 5, counting from 0. For a query patch (the patch that is reading), a head gives weights to the 196 patches and the class token. The weights are shares of the query's attention and add up to 1. The attention distance of the query is the average distance from the query to the patches, measured in patches, where a patch with a larger weight counts more. The mean distance of a head averages this over all queries and 14 photos.

  1. L2H5 and the query at row 6, column 6 (the coral square) start the figure. Read the boxes: 92% of the weight is on the 8 neighbours, 87% on the patch to the left, and the attention distance is 1.1 patches for this query.
  2. Choose L0H6, a head of block 0. Only 10% of the weight is on the neighbours. The attention distance is 4.9 patches for this query, and the mean distance of the head is 7.6.

In block 0, head L0H6 puts only 10% of this patch's weight on its 8 neighbours, and head L2H5 of block 2 puts 92%.

How it works

Take the query patch at row 6, column 6. The patches at row 6, column 9 and at row 9, column 10 are 3 and √(32 + 42) = 5 patches away. If a head gave all 196 patches the same weight, the attention distance of this query would be 5.38 patches, the mean of the 196 distances from this patch. Averaged over all queries it would be 7.28. The 12 heads of block 0 have mean distances of 6.7 to 7.6 patches, close to 7.28. Yet this does not mean even attention. For this query L0H6 gives its largest weight, 3%, to one patch, about six times the 0.5% that equal weights would give. Over all 144 heads, 8 have a mean distance below 3 patches and 101 have 6 or more.

\(\bar d(q)\)attention distance of query patch q=\(\sum_k a_{qk}\,\lVert\mathbf{p}_q-\mathbf{p}_k\rVert\)weight aqk on patch k times its distance in patches from q (p is a grid position), summed over k÷\(\sum_k a_{qk}\)the weight that falls on patches

Common belief. A bright patch in an attention map shows what the network used for its answer.

Why it fails. The map shows where one head reads from, for one query patch. As the class token section reports, flattening the last block's attention (equal weights on all 197 tokens) changes the hammerhead probability only from 88% to 81%. So for this photo the answer does not depend much on where that block's attention looks.

Better account. Treat the maps as a view of how information moves, and use occlusion, which hides part of the photo, to test what the answer needs.

Quick quiz

A head puts all its weight on the patch itself. What is its attention distance?

Zero patches. All terms of the sum have distance 0.

Why can a head with a large attention distance still be selective, that is, give most of its weight to a few patches?

It can give most of its weight to a few patches that lie far from the query. Attention distance measures where the weight falls, and it does not measure how concentrated the weight is.

Go deeper distances of all heads, symbols, Python about 4 min

Using the figure

The coral square is the query patch. The brightest patches get the most weight, and the shading is relative to the largest weight in the row.

Click a patch and switch heads. The six heads were picked by looking at the maps of all 144 heads for one query, to show the range. They are not an average, and other heads look different. The short descriptions of a head, such as "stays on the neighbours", say what its weights do for this query on these photos. They are descriptions of the maps and do not name a proven job of the head. The maps of single heads also differ from a gradient map, which shows how strongly a pixel changes the answer (the explaining chapter). The maps are stored at 16 levels, so shares are accurate to a point or two. The first row of boxes shows where the weight of this head goes: on the patch itself, on its eight neighbours, farther away, and on the class token. The second row gives the mean distance of the attention of this patch and of the whole head.

Distances of all 144 heads

The measured distances for all heads are in the next section. Of the 144 heads, 8 have a mean distance below 3 patches, 101 have 6 or more, and the other 35 lie between. A large mean distance does not mean even attention: for the query at row 6, column 6 the largest weight of L0H6 is 3%, against 0.5% for even attention. Four heads have a mean distance of 1.5 patches, the smallest of the 144: L2H5 and L2H10 in block 2, and L3H6 and L3H7 in block 3. Block 4 has four more heads below 3 patches. The last blocks are wide again.

Compared with the ViT paper

Dosovitskiy and others (2021) found, for their ViT-L/16, that some heads attend widely in low layers and others locally, and that distance grows with depth. This ViT-B/16 differs in two ways. All 12 heads of block 0 are wide, and the local heads appear later, in blocks 2 to 4. The mean distance of the 12 heads falls from 7.0 in block 0 to 4.3 in block 4 and then rises to 7.3 in block 11. The two networks differ in size and in training. The paper's model saw a far larger set than ImageNet-1k, and torchvision's weights used a DeiT-style recipe. The pattern depends on the network and its training, and this page does not test which factor matters.

A late head and background tokens

The late heads such as L7H6 put weight on a few patches of plain water. For the query at row 6, column 6, its largest weights fall on patches in the water at the top and bottom of the photo, and 19% of its weight goes to the class token. Darcet and others (2024) report high-norm tokens in background areas of other ViTs and show that they appear in the attention maps. This chapter did not test whether the same thing happens here.

Symbols

\[ \bar d(q) = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{N} a_{qk}\,\lVert \mathbf{p}_q - \mathbf{p}_k\rVert}{\sum_{k=1}^{N} a_{qk}} \]

  • \(a_{qk}\) is the attention weight of query patch \(q\) on patch \(k\) (D4). The sums skip the class token, so the denominator is the weight that falls on patches.
  • \(\mathbf{p}_q\) is the grid position (row, column) of patch \(q\), and \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) the straight-line distance in patches. The distance of a head is the average of \(\bar d(q)\) over all queries and 14 photos.

In Python

import numpy as np
g = 14
r, c = np.divmod(np.arange(g * g), g)                   # grid row and column of the 196 patches
q = 6 * g + 6                                           # the query patch at row 6, column 6
dist = np.hypot(r - r[q], c - c[q])                     # distance in patches from the query to every patch
even = np.full(g * g, 1 / (g * g))                      # even attention: the same weight on all patches
near = np.exp(-dist ** 2 / 2); near /= near.sum()       # made-up weights that fall off with distance
print(dist[6 * g + 9], dist[9 * g + 10])
print(round(float((even * dist).sum()), 2), round(float((near * dist).sum()), 2))
D = np.hypot(r[:, None] - r[None, :], c[:, None] - c[None, :])   # distances between all pairs of patches
print(round(float(D.mean()), 2))                        # even attention, averaged over all queries
3.0 5.0
5.38 1.21
7.28

The first line prints the distances of the two patches of the worked case. Even attention gives 5.4 for this query, which is near the middle of the photo. Over all queries it gives 7.3 on average, since a query near an edge is far from most patches. The made-up weights that fall off with distance give 1.2.

ViT against CNN

Guess first. A CNN is built to read nearby pixels. A ViT can read any patch from the first block. Which of the two needs more training photos to learn to recognise sharks, and why?

Inductive bias is what the design of a model assumes before it sees any data. A CNN assumes locality (nearby pixels belong together, so a convolution layer reads a small window) and weight sharing (one set of filters at all positions). Attention in a ViT, however, can read all tokens from the first block, so a ViT assumes less about where to look. In the ViT paper, ViT-Large did worse than ViT-Base when trained on ImageNet alone and better on a far larger set. The authors conclude that training on a large set can make up for the missing assumptions.

  1. Drag Layers stacked to 5: the left photo shows the 11 by 11 patch window of 5 stacked 3 by 3 convolution layers (farthest reach 7.1 patches). The right photo shows that one ViT block can read all 197 tokens.
  2. In the left chart the blue dots are the 144 heads of ViT-B/16 (12 per block), at 6.7 to 7.6 patches in block 0. The coral line is the farthest reach of k stacked layers, from k = 1 at the left.

Mean attention distance of the 144 heads of ViT-B/16, against the farthest reach of a CNN stack

Share of attention that falls inside the window, mean over heads

Stacked 3 by 3 convolutions need five to six layers before their farthest reach (7.1 to 8.5 patches) matches the average distance of ViT heads in block 0 (6.7 to 7.6).

How it works

Take 5 stacked 3 by 3 layers on the 14 by 14 patch grid. A 3 by 3 layer with a step of 1 and no pooling adds one patch on all sides, so 5 layers add 5. The receptive field, the part of the photo that can change one number of the last layer, is then 2 × 5 + 1 = 11 patches wide. Its farthest corner is 5√2 = 7.07 patches away. In block 0 of the ViT, only 5.8% of the attention falls on average in the 3 by 3 window around the query. Equal weights on all patches would put 4.2% there. So its heads read far beyond what one convolution layer sees. The next figure compares whole networks by the numbers learned, the work per photo and the accuracy.

5stacked 3 by 3 layers, k→11patches wide, 2k + 1→7.07farthest corner, k√2 patches|6.7 to 7.6mean attention distance of the 12 heads of block 0
  1. Under “Whole models” compare ViT-B/32 (P = 32) and ViT-B/16: they have 88.2 and 86.6 million numbers learned, but need 4.4 and 17.6 GFLOPs (billions of multiply-adds, in torchvision's counts). ViT-B/16 runs blocks of the same size over 197 tokens and ViT-B/32 over 50.
  2. Press “Inside ViT-B/16”: the 12 blocks contain 98.3% of the 86.6 million numbers, and the patch matrix 0.7%.

Common belief. Transformers replaced CNNs because they are better.

Why it fails. In the chart, ViT-B/16 gains 11 points of ImageNet accuracy over ResNet-18 (hover the bars) with about 7 times as many numbers and about 10 times the work. It was also trained with a different recipe (other training settings, such as how the photos were altered), so the gain does not come from the design alone.

Better account. The two designs make different assumptions, and which works better depends on the data, the compute and the task. Some models combine them, with convolutions in the first layers and attention above.

Quick quiz

What does a CNN assume that a ViT does not?

Locality (nearby pixels matter first) and the same filters at all positions, built into all layers. A ViT shares weights across tokens, but its attention can read any token from the first block.

ViT-B/32 and ViT-B/16 have almost the same number of weights. Why does ViT-B/16 cost about four times more work?

The weights are the same blocks. B/16 runs them over 197 tokens and B/32 over 50, and the work grows with the number of tokens (and with its square in attention).

Go deeper parameter counts, accuracy, what the data did, Python about 3 min

Reading the figure

The left picture is drawn from the design of the two networks. The CNN window grows by one patch on all sides with a 3 by 3 layer, so after k layers it is 2k + 1 patches wide (C2). The ViT picture is not a measurement: it says that in the first block a head can read all tokens. The blue dots of the first chart are measured. They give the mean attention distance of a head. The coral line is drawn from the design: the farthest that a stack of k layers reaches along the diagonal is k√2 patches. The second chart is measured too: it gives the share of attention that falls in a window. Five layers reach 7.1 patches and six reach 8.5, while block 0 heads attend 6.7 to 7.6 patches away on average.

Counting the parameters

A ViT block has 12d² + 13d = 7,087,872 numbers for d = 768. Of these, 2,362,368 are in attention, 4,722,432 in the MLP and 3,072 in two norms (the same block size as GPT-2 small in D5). Twelve blocks give 85,054,464, and with the patch matrix (590,592), the class token (768), the position table (151,296), the last norm (1,536) and the head (769,000) the total is 86,567,656. A 3 by 3 conv layer with 768 channels in and out has 5,309,184 numbers, which is more than the 2,362,368 of attention in a ViT block. Parameter counts do not tell the work. ViT-B/32 has 88.2 million numbers and ViT-B/16 has 86.6 million. The second needs 17.6 GFLOPs against 4.4 (torchvision's counts), since it runs the same blocks over 197 tokens and not 50.

Accuracy and recipes

All three ViTs in the chart have at least 3.3 times as many numbers as ResNet-50, and the ViT-B/16 does 17.6 GFLOPs of work where ResNet-18 does 1.8. The torchvision accuracy on ImageNet-1k is 69.8% (ResNet-18), 76.1% (ResNet-50), 75.9% (ViT-B/32), 81.1% (ViT-B/16) and 79.7% (ViT-L/16). The weights were trained with different recipes, so the chart compares packages and does not isolate the design.

What the data does

The ViT paper trained models on ImageNet alone, on ImageNet-21k and on JFT-300M. With ImageNet alone, ViT-Large did worse than ViT-Base. With the largest set, the large model did better. Its authors conclude that large-scale training outweighs the lack of an image bias (Dosovitskiy and others, 2021). This suggests that a CNN's locality helps when the training set is small, and that with a large set a ViT can learn such structure from the data. On a small robot (F2) the amount of work matters, since the compute is fixed. Suppose SharkCam had a few thousand photos: a pretrained network of either kind would be the starting point, and the fine-tuning of B7 would do the rest.

In Python

d = 768
conv3 = (3 * 3 * d + 1) * d            # a 3 by 3 convolution from 768 to 768 channels
attn = 4 * d * d + 4 * d               # W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O with their biases
mlp = d * 4 * d + 4 * d + 4 * d * d + d
norms = 2 * 2 * d
block = attn + mlp + norms
print(conv3, attn, mlp, block)

Discrete image tokens

Guess first. A text token is a whole number: an ID in a vocabulary (the tokenisation chapter). A patch token so far is a list of 768 numbers with decimals. If you wanted to give a language model the whole photo as a sentence, what would you need?

Vector quantisation replaces a vector by the nearest entry of a short list of vectors. The list is a code book of K vectors, the codes, with IDs from 0 to K − 1. The ID of the code that replaces a patch is the image token of that patch. In the figure a photo is cut into 28 × 28 = 784 patches of 8 by 8 pixels. The photo then becomes a sentence of 784 whole numbers, which a language model can read or write.

  1. Click a patch in either picture: the two small squares labelled patch and nearest code show the chosen patch and its code, and the line of text under the figure gives the image token. For the patch at row 10, column 12 the nearest of the 256 codes is #147.
  2. Press “4 codes”: the rebuilt picture has a few flat tones, 3 of the 4 codes are used, and the bits for the photo fall from 6,272 to 1,568.

Original, 28 × 28 patches of 8 × 8

Rebuilt from codes

The code book (dark tiles are unused for this photo)

patchnearest code

With 256 codes the 784 patches become 784 whole numbers and the picture is recognisable but blocky, and with 4 codes it is a few flat tones.

How it works

Count the bits. A bit is one 0 or 1, so n bits can name 2n values. A raw photo has 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 numbers and a number takes 8 bits, so the photo takes 1,204,224 bits. A code book of K = 256 codes needs log2 256 = 8 bits for an ID, because 28 = 256. So 784 tokens take 784 × 8 = 6,272 bits, which is 192 times smaller.

8bits per token, log2 K = log2 256×784tokens, 28 × 28 patches=6,272bits for the photo|1,204,224bits for the raw pixels|192 ×smaller

The nearest code is the one with the smallest squared distance. This is the sum of the squared differences of the 192 numbers (8 × 8 × 3) of the patch and the code. The code book comes from k-means, a method that groups similar 8 by 8 patches of 11 other photos into K groups, called clusters. The average patch of a group, its cluster centre, becomes one code.

Common belief. An image token is a piece of the picture.

Why it fails. In this figure a code is a stored 8 by 8 patch. In a learned system such as the VQ-VAE (van den Oord and others, 2017), a decoder (the part that rebuilds the picture) turns the codes into pixels together with their neighbours. So a code means “something like this goes here”. It cannot be read back into a patch without the decoder.

Better account. An image token is an ID in a vocabulary of visual words, chosen by closeness. Its meaning comes from the code book and the decoder, as the meaning of a text token comes from its embedding.

Quick quiz

A code book has 1,024 codes and a photo becomes 256 tokens. How many bits is the photo?

log2 1,024 = 10 bits per token, so 256 × 10 = 2,560 bits.

What is lost when a patch is replaced by its nearest code?

The detail that distinguishes the patch from its code, such as fine texture and small differences in colour. In the figure a larger code book loses less and costs more bits per token.

Go deeper symbols, learned code books, PSNR, Python about 3 min

Using the figure

Click a patch. The page finds the code with the smallest squared distance to the patch's 192 numbers, and the rebuilt picture uses the code's pixels. This is vector quantisation. The simplest way to make the code book is k-means: the code book is the set of K cluster centres. The fit is poor: details are gone, and many patches share one code. For the hammerhead photo with 256 codes only 33 codes are used. The readout gives the picture quality as PSNR, the peak signal-to-noise ratio in decibels, 10 log10(255² / mean squared error): it is 24.3 dB with 256 codes and 20.3 dB with 4, and a higher value means closer to the original. A code book is a dictionary, and the token is the dictionary entry, as with the subword vocabulary of D1. The difference is how an entry is chosen: by distance here, by merges in D1.

Symbols

\[ k^*(i) = \arg\min_{k\in\{0,\dots,K-1\}} \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{c}_k\rVert^2,\qquad \text{bits per token} = \log_2 K \]

  • \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is patch \(i\) as a list of numbers (192 for an 8 by 8 patch with three colours). \(\mathbf{c}_k\) is code \(k\) of the code book, and \(k^*(i)\) is the ID that becomes the image token.
  • \(\arg\min\) means "the \(k\) that makes the squared distance smallest". \(K\) is the number of codes, and \(\log_2 K\) is the number of bits needed to write one ID (8 bits for 256 codes).

Learned code books

The toy here works on raw pixels. Systems that make image tokens for language models learn the codes inside a network. In the VQ-VAE (van den Oord and others, 2017) an encoder network maps the photo to a grid of vectors. These vectors are replaced by their nearest entries of a learned code book, and a decoder rebuilds the picture from the entries. The nearest-entry step has no slope, so training copies the decoder's slope back to the encoder as if the step were not there. DALL-E (Ramesh and others, 2021) uses a related discrete autoencoder to compress a 256 by 256 photo into a 32 by 32 grid of tokens from a vocabulary of 8,192. This cuts the length that the transformer must model by a factor of 192. Esser and others (2021) learn the codes with a CNN and model the tokens with an autoregressive transformer, which is the next-token prediction of D3. A practical limit: some codes are used rarely or never (the dark tiles above), which wastes the book.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When a quantiser gives blurry pictures, count the codes used over many photos. If only a handful of the 256 are used, the code book has collapsed. The fix is in training (restart unused codes, or use a smaller code book) and the decoder is not at fault. The readout above gives this count for one photo only, and one photo can use few codes without any collapse.

In Python

import numpy as np
# vector quantisation of 2 by 2 grey patches (made-up numbers)
patches = np.array([[10, 12, 11, 9], [200, 210, 205, 198], [120, 20, 118, 25], [15, 14, 13, 12]], float)
book = np.array([[10, 10, 10, 10], [200, 200, 200, 200], [120, 20, 120, 20]], float)
d2 = ((patches[:, None, :] - book[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(2)
codes = d2.argmin(1)
print(codes)
print(np.round(np.sqrt(d2.min(1) / 4), 1))     # typical gap per number
print(np.log2(len(book)))                      # bits per token
[0 1 2 0]
[1.2 5.7 2.7 3.7]
1.584962500721156

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A ViT takes a 384 by 384 photo with P = 16. Find N, the sequence length n with a class token, the number of attention pairs per head, and the ratio to the 224 by 224 case. Then find the P at which the 384 photo gives the same N as the 224 photo with P = 16.

    Hint

    N = (S/P)². For the second part set (384/P)² = 196 and solve for P. Does P come out a whole number?

  2. theory Show that the patch matrix of a ViT is a convolution. Give the kernel size, the step, the number of output channels and the number of weights. Then say how many positions the output has for a 224 photo, using the output-size formula of C1.

  3. theory Prove that attention without position vectors is permutation-equivariant: if \(\Pi\) reorders the tokens, \(\mathrm{Attn}(\Pi X) = \Pi\,\mathrm{Attn}(X)\). Then say what changes when \(E_{\text{pos}}\) is added, and what would happen to the outputs if the whole photo were moved one patch to the right with wrap-around.

    Hint

    Write the score matrix as \(QK^\top\) with \(Q = XW_Q\). Reordering rows of \(X\) reorders the rows of \(Q\) and \(K\). What does a permutation matrix do to \(QK^\top\) and to softmax?

  4. theory A code book with K = 512 codes is used for patches of 16 by 16 pixels on a 224 photo. How many bits is the photo, how many times smaller than the raw pixels, and how many different token sentences are there?

Practice

  1. practice Write unpatchify(patches, S, P, C) in NumPy, the inverse of the cut in the first section, and check it with np.array_equal on a random image. Use it to move the patches of a picture according to a permutation of your choice.

  2. practice Compute the average distance between two random positions of a 14 by 14 grid (the value 7.3 in the figure). Then compute it for a 7 by 7 grid and for a 28 by 28 grid, and say how it grows with the side.

    Hint

    Build the coordinates with np.divmod(np.arange(g * g), g) and use broadcasting for all pairs.

  3. practice Write k-means with K = 8 on the 8 by 8 patches of a random-noise picture with a smooth gradient added, in NumPy only. Quantise the picture and plot the squared error against K = 2, 4, 8, 16. Is the curve smooth, and where does it stop being worth adding codes?

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam runs on a small computer and sees sharks that fill about 10% of a frame. You can choose P = 8, 16 or 32 on a frame resized to 224 by 224. What would you measure to choose, and what could go wrong? Think about the size of the animal in pixels, the cost per frame and what the figure on patches moved says about relying on layout.

  2. open The patches-moved test shows that the ViT keeps its top call in most runs when 32 patches are moved and in 29% when all are. Design a test to find out whether a shark detector built on a ViT uses the animal or the blue water. Say what you would change in the photos, what you would count, and how many photos you would need before you trusted a difference.

  3. open A discrete image token loses detail. Name two jobs where that is acceptable and two where it is unacceptable, for SharkCam. Say what you would check before choosing a code-book size.

Come back later

Answer after two days and again after a week, without looking back.

A ViT cuts a 224 by 224 photo with P = 16. Write down N, the numbers in a patch and the sequence length. Then say why halving P costs about 16 times more attention.

N = 196, 768 numbers in a patch, sequence length 197 with the class token. N grows 4 times, and attention costs grow with the square of the sequence, so about 16 times (cut, and the n² cost of D4).

The patch matrix is a convolution. Which numbers of a C1 filter correspond to its kernel size, stride and number of filters, and how does this tie to the embedding table of D2?

Kernel 16, stride 16, 768 filters. Like the D2 table, it turns an input into a vector of d numbers. It is a function of the patch and not a lookup (embed, C1, D2).

C3 shows that a classifier of ResNet-18 loses its shark calls in murky water. What would the patches-moved test tell you about whether a ViT would rely on the colour of the water, and what would it not tell you?

That the ViT keeps its call in some runs (29% at full move) when the layout is destroyed, so colour and texture of patches can give part of the answer. This is a warning that water colour could be a cue (B9, C3). It does not show that the water is the cue. That needs edits to the photos.
